column1: # Leaf contracts (UniSQL). One line per leaf id: `leaf<TAB>contract`. Lines starting `#` are comments.
# A leaf id never changes meaning; a change in meaning is a new id. A contract is the sentence a test
# must satisfy. "Same as the source" means: for the statement forms tested, the target returns the same
# rows (and, for writes, the same table state afterwards) as the source engine run on the source text.
# `<base>.<allowance>` leaves (a divergence a caller may accept) need no line of their own: the
# contract is the base leaf's, except that the divergence the named allowance describes
# (`Allowance` in crates/unisql-core/src/report.rs) is accepted. A base leaf that is `enabled=no,
# reason=wrong` in a matrix row is exactly the strict form of that sentence failing.
# Comparator canonicalisations (what "same" means when two results are compared by a test):
#   - booleans are read as 0/1 on both sides;
#   - a DECIMAL/NUMERIC value returned as text is compared as an integer when it has no fractional
#     part and as a double otherwise;
#   - an integer is never equal to a float (strict int-vs-float);
#   - result rows are compared as a multiset unless the case is marked ordered.
# Stronger implies weaker: where `<base>` is enabled, every `<base>.<allowance>` holds too.
# A leaf whose matrix row is `reason=missing` is a form the translator refuses; its contract below
# says what it would mean, and no backend has it on.

column2: `x = ANY($n)` / `x <> ALL($n)` with an array parameter gives the source's three-valued result, including NULL elements and a NULL array.
TRUE and FALSE literals evaluate and read back with the source's truth value.
CAST to a 64-bit integer returns the source's value; a malformed or out-of-range operand raises an error as at the source.
CAST to a double-precision float returns the source's value; a malformed operand raises an error as at the source.
CAST to a 32-bit integer returns the source's value; a malformed or out-of-range operand raises an error as at the source.
CAST to a timestamp without time zone yields the timestamp of the operand (a timestamptz is converted to the session zone); a malformed value raises an error.
CAST to text yields the source's text form of the operand.
CAST to a UUID yields a value of a UUID type that validates its input. Refused by every target that has no such type.
ARRAY[a, b, ...] is an array of the elements in order. Refused where there is no array type.
EXTRACT(DAY FROM x) is the day of the month of x.
EXTRACT(DOW FROM x) is the day of the week of x, 0 = Sunday. Refused where no mapping is verified.
EXTRACT(WEEK FROM x) is the ISO 8601 week number of x. Refused where no mapping is verified.
EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM a - b) is the number of seconds between the timestamps b and a (a - b).
EXTRACT(HOUR FROM x) is the hour (0-23) of x.
EXTRACT(MINUTE FROM x) is the minute (0-59) of x.
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM x) is the month (1-12) of x.
EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ts) is the number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC of the timestamp ts.
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM x) is the calendar year of x.
current_user is the name of the role the statement runs as. Refused where it has another form (MySQL user@host) or no equivalent.
ARRAY(SELECT ...) is an array of the single column of the query, in the query order. Refused where there is no array type.
ts AT TIME ZONE zone converts between timestamptz and a timestamp in the named zone. Refused where zone conversion differs or is unavailable.
`a || b` concatenates text; a NULL operand gives NULL.
WITH x AS (INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE ... RETURNING ...) ...: the modifying statement in the WITH runs once, its RETURNING rows are the CTE. Refused where only SELECT may appear in a WITH.
WITH ... DELETE ...: the common table expressions are visible to the DELETE. Refused where WITH may not precede a DELETE.
WITH ... INSERT ...: the common table expressions are visible to the INSERT. Refused where WITH may not precede an INSERT.
WITH ... UPDATE ...: the common table expressions are visible to the UPDATE. Refused where WITH may not precede an UPDATE.
`SELECT DISTINCT ON (keys) ...` keeps exactly one row per distinct key tuple, the first by ORDER BY; without ORDER BY which row survives is unspecified on both engines.
DISTINCT ON combined with a `*` projection. Refused: the emulation's helper columns would appear in the result.
`/` and `%` on the tested operands give the source's value; division by zero raises an error as at the source.
Division of two integers truncates toward zero and yields an integer.
`agg(...) FILTER (WHERE p)` aggregates only the rows for which p is true.
avg() over non-NULL inputs gives the source's mean and NULL over no rows.
btrim(s) removes leading and trailing spaces.
FROM generate_series(a, b[, step]) yields the integers (or timestamps) from a to b inclusive in order, one row each, column named by the alias. Refused where no mapping is verified.
char_length(s) is the number of characters of s.
date_trunc('day', ts) is ts cut to the start of its day.
date_trunc('hour', ts) is ts cut to the start of its hour.
date_trunc('minute', ts) is ts cut to the start of its minute.
date_trunc('month', ts) is ts cut to the start of its month.
date_trunc('week', ts) is ts cut to the start of its ISO week. Refused where no mapping is verified.
date_trunc('year', ts) is ts cut to the start of its year.
gen_random_uuid() is a random version-4 UUID in lower-case text form (8-4-4-4-12, version nibble 4, variant 8/9/a/b); two calls give different values.
coalesce(a, b, ...) returns the first non-NULL argument.
concat(a, b, ...) treats NULL arguments as empty strings. Refused where the target's CONCAT returns NULL if any argument is NULL.
convert_to(s, enc) returns the bytes of s in encoding enc. Refused where no such function is built in.
count(x) counts non-NULL x; count(*) counts rows.
current_schema() names the session's current schema. Refused where there is no such catalog.
date_format(ts, fmt) formats a timestamp by a MySQL format string. Refused: no verified mapping.
instr(s, t) is the 1-based position of t in s, 0 if absent. Refused: no verified mapping.
CURRENT_DATE is the date of the current day in the session time zone.
lag(x) OVER (...) is x of the previous row in the window.
lead(x) OVER (...) is x of the next row in the window.
length(s) is the number of characters of s.
lower(s) maps every character of s to lower case.
ltrim(s) removes leading spaces.
make_interval(...) builds an interval from named parts. Refused where month/year arithmetic differs.
make_interval(..) used on its own, not as the right operand of a timestamp +/-. Refused by every target without an interval type.

make_interval(months|years => n) added to or subtracted from a timestamp. Refused by every target that does not give the source engine's end-of-month behaviour; the fixed-length units (secs, mins, hours, days, weeks) are `fn:make_interval`.
max(x) is the greatest non-NULL x under the source's ordering of x.
md5(s) is the lower-case hexadecimal MD5 digest of the bytes of s. Refused where no hashing is built in.
min(x) is the least non-NULL x under the source's ordering of x.
now() is the start time of the current transaction as a timestamp with time zone.
nullif(a, b) is NULL when a = b, else a.
octet_length(s) is the number of bytes of s in the database encoding.
random() is a value in [0, 1). Refused: no verified mapping.
rank() OVER (...) is the rank with gaps of the row within its partition.
regexp_replace(s, pattern, repl) replaces the first match of a POSIX pattern. Refused where there is no regular-expression function.
replace(s, from, to) replaces every occurrence of from by to.
row_number() OVER (...) numbers the rows of a partition from 1 in window order.
strftime(fmt, ts) formats a timestamp by a SQLite format string. Refused: no verified mapping.
string_agg(x, sep) concatenates the non-NULL x with sep between them; NULL over no rows.
string_agg(x, sep ORDER BY k) concatenates in the order given by k.
substr(s, start[, len]) is the substring from the 1-based start. Refused where start positions before 1 behave differently.
sum(x) over non-NULL inputs gives the source's total and NULL over no rows.
sum(x ORDER BY k): an aggregate with an ORDER BY clause. Refused by every target that cannot honour the ordering inside the aggregate.
to_regclass(name) resolves a relation name in the catalog. Refused where there is no such catalog.
typeof(x) names the storage class of x. Refused: no verified mapping.
to_timestamp(seconds) is the timestamp that many seconds after 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.
upper(s) maps every character of s to upper case.
`a ILIKE p` is a case-insensitive LIKE with `%` and `_` wildcards.
`ts +/- make_interval(secs => n)` shifts a timestamp by n seconds.
INNER JOIN returns the pairs of rows satisfying the condition.
LEFT JOIN returns every left row, with NULLs where no right row matches.
`doc -> key` yields the JSON value at key.
`doc ->> key` yields the value at key as text, NULL when absent.
`a LIKE p` is a case-sensitive pattern match with `%` and `_` wildcards.
LIMIT n returns at most n rows of the ordered result.
`f(name => value)` calls a function with a named argument. Refused where function arguments are positional only.
NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST places NULLs as stated; the default places NULLs last for ASC and first for DESC.
a <=> b is true when both are NULL or equal, false when exactly one is NULL, never NULL.
INSERT IGNORE skips a row whose unique key already exists and inserts the others.
a || b between conditions is logical OR with the lowest precedence (MySQL default sql_mode).
SUBSTRING(s, pos[, len]) with pos >= 1 and len >= 0 is the substring from the 1-based pos.
OFFSET n skips the first n rows of the ordered result.
ORDER BY orders by the keys, ascending unless stated, comparing text bytewise in the C locale.
`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and BETWEEN compare two values; text compares bytewise in the C locale.
WITH RECURSIVE evaluates the recursive term to a fixed point and returns its rows.
RETURNING returns the affected rows after the statement's changes.
UPDATE ... RETURNING returns the updated rows. Refused where RETURNING is not supported on UPDATE.
FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until the transaction ends. Refused where there are no row locks.
FOR UPDATE/SHARE ... NOWAIT raises an error at once when a selected row is locked by another transaction, and behaves as without NOWAIT when none is.
FOR UPDATE/SHARE OF <table> locks only the rows of that table in a join. Refused where unsupported.
FOR SHARE takes a shared lock on the selected rows until the transaction ends. Refused where there is no such clause.
FOR UPDATE/SHARE ... SKIP LOCKED leaves rows locked by another transaction out of the result and locks the rest.
`=` and `<>` on text compare bytewise (the C locale).
trim(chars FROM s) removes the single character chars (or spaces) from the stated side(s).
trim with a set of several characters. Refused where the target trims a repeated string instead of a set.
UPDATE ... FROM joins other tables into the update. Refused where unsupported.
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE/NOTHING resolves a conflict on the stated key.
An upsert that states no conflict key. Refused where the target needs the key columns.
ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ... WHERE applies the update only when the condition holds. Refused where there is no WHERE on the conflict action.
`f(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)` evaluates over each partition in order.
